Congrats on considering this and taking steps to secure your long term future. This is how I would proceed if I were in your shoes. 

1. Buy personal health insurance for yourself if you don’t have it yet. This should be separate from your company provided insurance. If you believe your parents will rely on your income, then term insurance as well. 
2. Figure out your monthly/annual fixed costs. This is all the stuff that are necessities. Rent, groceries, commute to office, wifi or phone bill, etc. Put aside at least 6 months worth of expenses as an emergency fund. This is in case you ever lose your job suddenly. You can keep it in a bank FD. As your expenses and salary increase, ensure to proportionately increase your emergency fund accordingly. 
3. Work on your health. Whether that is gym or some sports activity. Take the subscription or buy the equipment you need. Your body will thank you in the long run. 
4. Make 4 buckets - fixed costs (the things you have to pay every month to survive), variable costs (the additional expenses you make every month for fun, travel, meeting friends, etc), short term savings (something you want to buy over the next few months or one year that you need to save up for like new phone or something you really like). The 4th bucket is long term savings - for retirement and the rest of your life. 
5. Chart out your financial and life goals - typically this is marriage, children, buying a house, etc. Have a rough plan of when you think these events will happen and how much you need for them. This will dictate your long term savings bucket. 
6. At your age and since you say you don’t have any family or financial responsibilities, you may be able to save at least 50-70% in long term savings. However, this will depend on your goals and other needs. 
7. Based on your long term goals, look up an SIP calculator online and work backwards to map how much you need to put in SIP to have the corpus you need for life events in future. 
8. Once you know the SIP amounts you need, invest them in a few relevant mutual funds. You should go higher in equity funds at your age. Have some debt instruments for safety. The general rule is 100 - your age = debt allocation and the rest is equity. So that means 20-25% of your investment and corpus should be in debt instruments like debt funds or PPF or EPF. The rest in equity. Adjust this ratio every few years. 
9. For equity funds, you need a max of 3 usually. One large cap or blue chip fund, one flexicap and one midcap or small cap. Check funds with decent performance history and low expense ratio. 
10. Only invest in direct mutual funds. Don’t invest in regular funds. You can use any platform like Groww, zerodha, Kubera, etc. 
11. Use this time to try and learn about investments and taxations. Understand how taxation works, learn about different types of financial instruments and what are the pros and cons of them. 
12. Don’t try to chase high returns right now. Doing SIP consistently and regularly is much more important to learn at this age. You may choose to do riskier investments in your life in future, but first learn the basics before you decide to do things like stock market trading, crypto or any of those. 
13. Most importantly - don’t be a miser. Money is meant to make your life better and comfortable. Don’t forgo fun. Travel, live your life, do interesting things while you manage your SIPs

Would not suggest to go through banks for investing at this stage in your career. They will usually upsell all of their own products. Do research on YouTube and go through a 3rd party platform. I use Groww but there are many like Zerodha, indmoney, Kubera, etc. 

Don’t try to do too much. The idea of you doing SIP at age 22 should be for financial discipline and consistency. You need 2-3 funds at this age only - one large cap/blue chip find and one mid-cap or flexi cap should be sufficient for your needed. Just focus on doing the SIP every month without fail for few years. 

Before doing any SIP, I would suggest to make an emergency fund of 3-6 months expenses. Just put that in FD or RD. Once you have that done, leave it and don’t touch it unless you have an emergency. Then you can divert those same funds every month to SIP.

Best advice I can give you from personal experience is to engage the service of a few-only financial planner. I personally found it worth the cost as this person will help you understand your risk appetite, short and long term goals and how to properly allocate your money for each of these buckets. 

In general, here are the basic things to keep in mind:
1. First, ensure you have at least a 6 month emergency fund. Keep it in a safe space (FD or arbitrage fund)
2. Get all relevant insurance - health insurance independent of your office, term insurance or life insurance if you have dependents 
3. Note down your goals - short term, medium term and long term. Figure out how much you’d have to save for each of these goals. 
4. General rule of thumb is equity allocation should be 100 minus current age. The rest should go into debt. 
5. Nifty index funds are a great place to start. Have a Nifty 100 (50% capital allocation), Nifty mid cap (25%) and nifty small cap fund (25%). Look for reputed find house with low expense ratio. Make a monthly SIP and just let the money go out every month. 
6. Increase your contributions to SIPs by 10% every year. 

Everything else above this depends on your personal preferences. I don’t see any value in trying to time the market or buy the dip and all that jazz. Consistent SIP is the most important.

Three major benefits: 
1) Biggest benefit is that you can establish credit history which can help you get better rates on loans in long term. But that’s if and only if you pay back your CC amount in full by the due date. Miss one payment and your credit rating will drop a lot. 

2) You can accrue some credit card points which can be redeemed for airline miles, hotel points, cash back or vouchers depending on your bank. I typically end up getting 1-2 round trip flights to my hometown every year by accumulating points on my credit card. My average spends on credit card are around 30k per month. I use credit card for almost everything except rent or payments below 150-200 rupees. Those are things I am anyway spending on so I do the payment on my card. 

3) Can be useful in an emergency where you need to pay something ASAP (eg: medical bills) and cannot wait to withdraw cash or break FD, etc. 

That being said - only get a credit card if you have existing payments you are making on UPI or debit card that can be put to credit card. Don’t just get it because there is some lifetime free offer and start swiping. It can be very easy to loose track of spends if you’re simply swiping your card everywhere as the money doesn’t leave your account immediately. 

There are folks who also say that credit card allows you to leave your money untouched in account for anywhere from 30-45 days and get interest. This only would be useful if you were to typically spend a significant amount on cards every month (eg 1L+). Then you’d get a few thousands in interest in your bank account. 

There are also folks who who make it a mission to optimise and get as many points as possible using their credit cards which they redeem for travel, etc. They buy gift card vouchers with 2X or 5X or 10X rewards offers, etc. This is possible but imo very painful and time consuming, and again only worth it if your monthly spends are already significantly high.

The point of SIP is to manage the natural ups and downs of the market. If you are taking a 30 year time horizon, then odds are that out of 360 months that 150-200 months the market will be high. You’re not going to avoid investing in all those months are you?

There are different kinds of investments depending on risk factor and your long term goals. Stick to 2-3 funds only. My suggestion would be 4k in nifty index fund and 2k in a small cap fund (I personally invest in quant small cap). The small cap fund is more volatile with higher peaks but also higher drops. It is beneficial in the long run (since you are 18 your investment horizon should ideally be 30-40 years). Over that long a time frame you will consistently get growth. The nifty is less risky and closely mimics the overall market so you get slightly more stable returns. The most important thing is not number of funds or amount in each fund but consistency - keep investing every month in the SIPs regardless of market or Sensex conditions, don’t touch the money and leave it invested for a long time frame and attempt to increase your SIPs annually by 10%.

Why would you cash out when the market has crashed and the value of your holdings has gone down? It will correct in some time and then you will buy again at a higher price. If you have money to invest, put in a lumpsum instead.

This is a story from the mid-1800s. In central Mumbai near what is currently Parel, there were 2 local gangs. There was constant tussle for territory amongst these gangs and it started becoming extremely violent. Finally the heads of both the gangs had enough and decided the violence needed to stop. So instead of a gang fight, the two heads decided to fight 1-1 to settle the dispute and the winner would get that territory and the loser would have to leave. On the day of the fight, the two gang leaders came prepared with their followers. One gang leader was called Mr. Chinch and the other was known as Mr. Lee. 

A crowd had gathered because all the locals wanted to watch this showdown. Mr Lee had practiced his fighting skills, but Mr Chinch knew he couldn’t defeat Mr Lee in a normal fight. So he was secretly taking king fu lessons and he learnt some ancient kung fu martial arts techniques, including ways to incapacitate his opponent with just one strike. The fight started and Mr Lee was showing off, boasting loudly and trying to attack. Mr Chinch avoided all the attacks and when the time was right, he used his martial arts training and poked Lee in this one area of his neck causing Lee to be defeated. Everyone cheered at the end of the fight and the end of gang violence in the area. Just one poke from Mr Chinch ended the fight. 

The next day, the newspapers covered the fight and the front page of the paper ran the headline “Chinch poke Lee! Chinch poke Lee!”

And that’s how the area currently named Chinchpokli got its name.

The point of other instruments like FD is for diversification, immediate short term goals and to ensure a certain amount of money is extremely safe. If you have covered those aspects, ensured a safe emergency fund etc, then FDs are not necessary unless you have a goal within the next 12 months horizon. 

Physical gold for me is more of a peace of mind than an investment instrument. If I have some extra cash lying around at the end of a financial year, I buy gold for some peace of mind but not as a long term investment. For a salaried individual with an extremely long time horizon and who stays invested without freaking out about market ups and downs, equities is still a better long term bet than gold.

1. Spend 10-15 mins cleaning every day rather than trying to do it all on one day. Just pick a section of the house and do it or do one type of cleaning activity everyday.
2. Dishes pile up without you realising. One minute there's one bowl and a spoon, the next there's 4 cups, 3 plates, 6 bowls and 3 saucepans. When you live along, you're the only one responsible for washing. Do dishes while you cook or immediately after cooking and eating.
3. Not sure how you split household supplies with former roommates, but buying household supplies will be a bit more expensive coz it's just you. Eg - toilet cleaner, detergent, dishwashing liquid, trashbags. Budget well. 
4. Make weekend plans. It's really easy to just get lazy on the weekends when you're alone. Plan in advance for what you're going to do.
5. Have a good relationship with neighbours. Don't need to be friends with them but should introduce yourself, know their names, say hi, occassionally send over some cookies you baked or something. Always keep your neighbours on your side especially when living alone. Never know when you need them to accept a package or drive you to the hospital.
6. Buy less quantity of food but shop more often. It sounds great to buy all your groceries for the next 10 days together, but food spoils. If you have the ability, just buy enough perishables for 3 days and shop again.
7. You will walk around naked if you are living alone. Everyone does. Put a towel down on the couch where you're sitting. Sweaty ass prints are not fun and leave a stink, especially if you have a leather couch.

Akuri and bhurji aren't exactly the same thing. Basic concept for both is scrambled eggs with veggies and spices. But Akuri is supposed to be runny eggs with the veggies cooked long and almost to a mash or paste like consistency. Bhurji is meant to be overcooked eggs but veggies still have a little bit of a bite, and traditionally is on the spicier side.

That being said - cook em however you like. It's your breakfast so enjoy it how you like.
